slides.title: Why a Fair Gamble Feels Unfair
slides.content_summary: vNM: rational investors maximize E[u(W)], not E[W]. Concave u ⟹ the chord lies below the curve ⟹ E[u(W)] < u(E[W]) (Jensen). Student widens a 50/50 gamble around the same mean and watches expected utility fall.

visual_spec.student_actions: Drag a spread slider; curve u(W)=√W with chord, E[u] point, u(E[W]) point, CE and π bracket update live.
visual_spec.ties_to_concept: Curvature IS risk aversion; the gap is Jensen's inequality.

slides.lux_integration: Lux asks: 'The mean never moved — why did your utility fall?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Guide to: concavity means gains add less utility than equal losses remove. Introduce A(W)=−u''/u' only if asked.

slides.title: Certainty Equivalent & Risk Premium
slides.content_summary: u(CE)=E[u(W)]; π=E[W]−CE; Pratt π ≈ ½A(W)σ². Utility families: quadratic, CRRA, CARA, log. Why MV analysis works: quadratic u OR jointly normal returns.
slides.lux_integration: Lux can quiz: 'Which family has constant RELATIVE risk aversion?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Pratt approximation is for small fair gambles; π scales linearly in variance and in A(W).

slides.title: Your Turn: Price the Gamble
slides.content_summary: Log-utility investor faces 50/50 wealth of $50 or $150. Compute CE and π.

problem_spec.scenario: u(W)=ln W; W = $50 or $150, each with probability 1/2.

slides.lux_integration: Hints ladder: (1) write E[u] first; (2) invert the log with exp; (3) π is a subtraction.
slides.system_prompt_notes: Do NOT reveal CE=86.60 unless the student has attempted. Common error: computing u(E[W])=ln 100 instead of E[u(W)].

slides.title: Rankings Everyone Agrees On: FSD & SSD
slides.content_summary: FSD: F_A ≤ F_B everywhere (shift right) — unanimous for all who prefer more. SSD: integrated CDF condition (shift + mean-preserving spread) — unanimous for the risk-averse. Same-mean normals: SSD ⟺ lower variance.

visual_spec.student_actions: Toggle FSD/SSD mode; drag B's shift and spread; verdict banner states whether dominance holds and for which investor class.

slides.lux_integration: Lux asks: 'Make the CDFs cross — which dominance concept just died, and which might survive?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: FSD implies SSD, not conversely. SSD tie-in is the bridge to mean–variance.

slides.title: Two Numbers That Do Most of the Work
slides.content_summary: Mean and variance, discrete and continuous. The normal: ±1σ→68.26%, ±2σ→95.50%; standardization. Sample estimates: x̄, s² with T−1, SE(x̄)=σ/√T — doubling precision quadruples the sample.
slides.system_prompt_notes: If returns are normal, (E,σ) pin down the whole distribution — this is why MV is the right framework, not a shortcut.

slides.title: Are Returns Actually Normal?
slides.content_summary: Skewness (equities: negative), kurtosis (normal=3; daily returns much higher), studentized range. Fama (1965): a 4σ day should occur once in 50 years; reality ≈ four times every five years. Logs for compounding; lognormal moments E[r]=e^{μ+σ²/2}−1.
slides.lux_integration: Lux asks: 'Flip on fat tails — where does the probability mass come from?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Cross-section: simple returns ~ normal. Time series: log returns ~ normal ⟹ simple lognormal ⟹ no negative prices.

slides.title: Your Turn: Mean & Volatility from a Scenario Table
slides.content_summary: Three-state stock return: −10% (p=0.3), +5% (p=0.4), +20% (p=0.3). Compute E[r] and σ(r).
slides.system_prompt_notes: Common error: forgetting to square deviations, or using T−1 (this is a POPULATION/probability-weighted calc, not a sample).

slides.title: Weights, Portfolio Return, Covariance
slides.content_summary: w_j = dollars in j over portfolio value; Σw=1; R_p=WᵀR; E[R_p]=Wᵀμ. Two-asset variance w₁²σ₁²+w₂²σ₂²+2w₁w₂σ₁₂; ρ=σ₁₂/(σ₁σ₂).
slides.system_prompt_notes: The cross term is where all the interesting economics lives.

slides.title: The Only Free Lunch: Turn the ρ Dial
slides.content_summary: Lecture example: two stocks, σ²=0.04 each, 50/50 ⟹ σ²_p = 0.02+0.02ρ. Slider from +1 to −1: 0.04 → 0. N-asset view: σ²_p = WᵀVW; N=100 means 9,900 covariances vs 100 variances — covariance drives portfolio risk.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'At ρ=0 you halved variance without giving up a basis point of expected return. Who paid for that?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: ρ=−1 fully hedges. Emphasize: diversification cuts variance, never the mean.

slides.title: Your Turn: Two-Asset Portfolio Risk
slides.system_prompt_notes: Common errors: forgetting the factor 2; using ρ where σ₁₂ belongs; not converting % to decimals consistently.

slides.title: One Risky Asset: The Capital Allocation Line
slides.content_summary: T-bills rf=5.5%; S&P E=7.9%, σ=12.1% (lecture numbers). E[R_p]=w·7.9+(1−w)·5.5; σ_p=w·12.1. Slider past w=1 is leverage. Slope everywhere = Sharpe = (7.9−5.5)/12.1 ≈ 0.198.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Slide to w=1.3 — what are you doing with the −30%?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Utility U=E−αS² and indifference curves pick the point on the CAL; higher α ⟹ closer to rf.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Optimal Risky Share
slides.content_summary: Derivation recap: max (1−ω)rf+ωE_P−αω²S_P² ⟹ ω*=(E_P−rf)/(2αS_P²). With E_P=7.9%, rf=5.5%, σ_P=12.1%, α=2: find ω*.
slides.system_prompt_notes: Units trap: σ must be squared in DECIMALS (0.121²=0.014641). If student gets 0.41 in decimals accept it.

slides.title: Two Risky Assets: The Curve Bends with ρ
slides.content_summary: Assets (σ=18,E=6) and (σ=15,E=12) from the lecture figure. ρ slider: +1 straight, 0 bowed, −1 touches the E-axis (riskless combo). MVP = leftmost point.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'At ρ=−1, find the weight that makes σ exactly zero.' (w₁·18=w₂·15 ⟹ w₁=15/33≈45.5%)
slides.system_prompt_notes: Bending left = diversification benefit made visible.

slides.title: Many Assets: Bullet, MVP, Tangency
slides.content_summary: Feasible region is a bullet; left edge a hyperbola; only the upper branch (above MVP) is efficient — every lower point has a same-σ, higher-E twin. Add rf: the ray from rf tangent to the frontier has max Sharpe; tangency point T. Two-fund separation: everyone holds T, only the T-vs-rf mix differs.
slides.system_prompt_notes: This slide is the geometric heart of the course; CAPM will rename T as the market.

slides.title: The Frontier in Closed Form
slides.content_summary: min WᵀVW s.t. WᵀR=r_p, Wᵀ1=1. Lagrangian ⟹ W*=V⁻¹[R 1]A⁻¹(r_p,1)ᵀ with A=[R 1]ᵀV⁻¹[R 1]=[[a,b],[b,c]] (a=RᵀV⁻¹R, b=1ᵀV⁻¹R, c=1ᵀV⁻¹1). Frontier: σ²_p=(a−2b·r_p+c·r_p²)/(ac−b²).
slides.system_prompt_notes: Students often fear this derivation; the payoff is that THREE scalars pin down the whole frontier.

slides.title: Three Numbers Rule the Frontier
slides.content_summary: Drag a, b, c; the parabola σ(r_p) redraws; MVP marker rides at r=b/c with σ=1/√c. Remarkable property: Cov(any portfolio, MVP)=1/c.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Double c holding b/c fixed — what happened to the minimum risk and why?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: r_MVP=b/c from dσ²/dr=0; σ²_MVP=1/c. Equal-covariance property is a diagnostic for the MVP.

slides.title: Your Turn: Locate the MVP
slides.content_summary: Given a=0.20, b=2.0, c=25 (annual, decimal returns): find r_MVP and σ_MVP.

slides.title: MVP vs Tangency: The Two Formulas to Remember
slides.content_summary: W_MVP=V⁻¹1/(1ᵀV⁻¹1) — equal covariance with every asset. W_T=V⁻¹(R−rf1)/(1ᵀV⁻¹(R−rf1)) — equal (E[r_i]−rf)/Cov(r_i,R_T) across assets. Two-fund separation and the beta representation R=rf1+β(r_T−rf) — the CAPM's skeleton.
slides.system_prompt_notes: MVP needs only V; tangency needs means too — this asymmetry becomes the punchline of Block F.

blocks.block_title: When Optimization Meets Data: Estimation Risk

slides.title: Jorion (1992): The Error Maximizer
slides.content_summary: MV treats μ̂, V̂ as truth. The optimizer piles onto the highest estimated means and friendliest estimated covariances — exactly the noisiest inputs. Jorion's global bonds 1978–88: the top frontier point put 98% in Japanese Yen. Fixes: constraints (no shorts, position limits) and... simulation.
slides.system_prompt_notes: 'Error maximizer' framing: optimization amplifies sampling error into corner solutions.

slides.title: Run Jorion's Experiment Yourself
slides.content_summary: The 7-step recipe live: draw simulated histories from the estimated MVN, re-optimize each, evaluate every simulated tangency at the TRUE parameters, plot the cloud. Toggle short sales: Figure A (tight cloud) becomes Figure C (explosion). GRS F-test measures whether a benchmark is statistically distinguishable from efficient. Punchline: MVP is easier to estimate than tangency — it needs only V, and second moments are better estimated than means.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'Your in-sample Sharpe went UP when you allowed shorts. Why should that scare you?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: Evaluate simulated weights at ACTUAL parameters — students routinely miss this step. GRS: F=[T(T−N−1)/(N(T−2))]·(θ*²−θp²)/(1+θp²).

slides.title: From Tangency to the CAPM
slides.content_summary: Tangency property: (E[r_i]−rf)/Cov(r_i,R_T) equal across assets ⟹ apply to T itself ⟹ E[r_i]=rf+β_i(E[R_T]−rf) with β_i=Cov/Var. Equilibrium (homogeneous beliefs, MV investors, rf borrowing/lending): everyone holds T, supply=demand ⟹ T IS the market portfolio. Marginal — not average — contribution to risk is what's priced.
slides.system_prompt_notes: The economic intuition: prices set at the margin, like marginal cost in micro.

slides.title: The Security Market Line
slides.content_summary: SML: E[r]=rf+β(E[R_M]−rf). Drag β; place an asset above (undervalued, positive α) or below (overvalued) the line. Applications: cost of capital, fund evaluation, event studies, efficiency tests.
slides.lux_integration: Lux: 'An asset sits above the SML. What trade does every MV investor want, and what does that do to its price?'
slides.system_prompt_notes: β is a regression slope of r_i on R_M. α>0 above the line.

slides.title: Your Turn: Price an Asset with the CAPM
slides.content_summary: rf=3%, E[R_M]=9%, β=1.4: required return? Then: the stock's forecast return is 12% — over- or under-valued?

problem_spec.verification: E[r]=3+1.4·(9−3)=3+8.4=11.4%. Forecast 12% > 11.4% ⟹ positive alpha of 0.6% ⟹ undervalued.

slides.system_prompt_notes: Common error: using E[R_M] instead of the premium (E[R_M]−rf). Follow-up (Socratic, not graded): what does buying pressure do to price and expected return?

new_problem_templates.answer_rule: CE = exp(p·ln W_high + (1−p)·ln W_low); π = E[W] − CE
